stewart_read: Rep reads an address that the customer never confirms cleanly before switching to a completely different address, and this mismatch is never reconciled.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep could have been reading from a lead record that was simply wrong, making this a data problem rather than a rep skill problem — but the rep still doesn't stop to reconcile it.
coaching_implication: Rep should pause and confirm 'is that the same property you're about to give me, or a different one?' before proceeding.

quote: Okay. So we don't do solar on apartments.
stewart_read: The DQ is delivered flatly with no acknowledgment of the customer's effort spelling out her address, and no attempt to check if she owns any qualifying property.
alternative_hypothesis: If Ion genuinely never does solar on any apartment regardless of ownership, the DQ itself may be correct policy — but the rep still owed her a probe on the rental house she mentioned.
coaching_implication: Before closing out, ask 'do you own any other property — like that rental house — that might qualify instead?'

quote: It's also a rental house as well.
stewart_read: Customer hands the rep a second potential lead (a rental house she may own) and the rep never asks a single clarifying question about it.
coaching_implication: This is a live, unprobed lead — 'is that rental house yours? Do you own it?' should have been the very next line.

stewart_read: Rep has no fallback resource or referral list when asked who services apartments, leaving the customer without help of any kind.
coaching_implication: Even a DQ'd customer deserves a professional close — rep should have a stock line ready rather than 'I have no idea.'

stewart_read: The customer, not the rep, supplies the competitor name; the rep simply echoes it back instead of offering any real guidance or closing professionally.
coaching_implication: Even in a DQ, rep should own the close with a clear, confident sign-off rather than letting the confused customer script the ending.
